Romania and the Republic of Moldova, from dialogue to investments: F.E.R.M. builds new economic bridges over the Prut River Economics News Latest News Published on September 21, 2026 By Magda Purice Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email The second edition of the Economic Forum Romania-Republic of Moldova F.E.R.M. , organized by the European Employers’ Association of Business Women – PEFA, under the aegis of the National Bank of Moldova, in institutional partnership with the Embassy of Romania in the Republic of Moldova and with the support of AFAM and AIR, brought together in Chisinau representatives of public authorities, the diplomatic environment, the financial-banking sector, industry, infrastructure, research and entrepreneurial environment from the two states. The event marked a new step in strengthening the economic relations between Romania and the Republic of Moldova and created the framework for an applied dialogue on investments, financing, innovation, internationalization of companies and the development of joint projects on the two banks of the Prut. At the official opening of the F.E.R.M., Anca Dragu, Governor of the National Bank of Moldova, spoke about the role of the financial-banking system in capitalizing on the bilateral economic potential: “The economic cooperation between the Republic of Moldova and Romania has an important potential, and the financial-banking system can contribute decisively to capitalizing on it. Stability, transparency and trust are the foundation of sustainable investments. It is essential to develop modern financing instruments, to facilitate entrepreneurs’ access to capital and to encourage initiatives capable of generating added value, competitiveness and long-term development.” The Forum also presented the conclusions of the Female Entrepreneurship and Leadership Index, a study conducted by PEFA, which highlighted the points of convergence between the business environments in Romania and the Republic of Moldova, as well as the economic potential that can be capitalized through closer cooperation. In the FinanciarELE panel, moderated by the Governor of the NBM and with Natalia Bejan, Director of the Moldovan Investment Agency, as a guest, the discussions also addressed the economic cost of gender inequality and the impact of women’s access to finance and decision-making positions on the competitiveness of the economy. “At the National Bank of Moldova we support initiatives that encourage a wider participation of women in the economy and in the decision-making process. Because a modern European economy is built through competence, trust and equal opportunities to contribute to its development,” said Anca Dragu. Andreea Negru, president of the European Business Women’s Employers’ Association – PEFA, underlined the objective of the F.E.R.M. to evolve from an annual event to a permanent platform for economic cooperation: “Romania and the Republic of Moldova are united by history, language, culture and common values. However, we have the responsibility to transform this rapprochement into a real economic force, capable of generating investments, jobs and prosperity on both banks of the Prut. The second edition of the Forum has shown us that there is interest, energy and openness for building sustainable partnerships. We want the Romania-Republic of Moldova Economic Forum to become a permanent platform for dialogue, where we will present, from one year to the next, not only intentions, but also investments made, companies developed and successful projects built together.” Present at the Forum, His Excellency Cristian-Leon Țurcanu, Ambassador of Romania to the Republic of Moldova, said: “Strengthening the economic ties between the two banks of the Prut is not business as usual. It is a strategic objective: more interconnection, more investments, more joint projects and deeper economic integration. We already have a strong investment presence and an ever-growing entrepreneurial interest on both sides of the Prut. The next step is to transform this energy into joint projects, long-term investments and value chains that will integrate us more and more deeply into the European market.” Lorena Stoian, First Vice-President of PEFA, highlighted the importance of the direct relationship between the entrepreneurial environment and institutions: “Entrepreneurship is built through trust, collaboration and the ability to bring people, ideas and opportunities together. Through F.E.R.M. we have created a space for dialogue between entrepreneurs, companies and institutions from Romania and the Republic of Moldova, from which partnerships and concrete projects can be born. Because the true measure of F.E.R.M.’s success is what we manage to build together after the end of the event.” Present at the official opening, MP Vali Priceputu, Deputy Chairman of the Committee on Entrepreneurship and Tourism of the Chamber of Deputies, said: “The Romania-Republic of Moldova Economic Forum responds to a real need for dialogue and cooperation between the business environments of the two states. I want this initiative to become a permanent platform and that, every year, we will meet again in Chisinau to present the results of the partnerships started in previous editions: investments made, companies developed, newly created jobs and successful businesses built together. Romania will continue to be a firm partner of the Republic of Moldova in its European path and in the process of economic consolidation.” Another important topic of the Forum was the role of technology, research and digitalization in increasing the competitiveness of companies and modernizing the administration. Victor Vevera, General Manager of ICI Bucharest, said: “Digital transformation can accelerate cooperation between Romania and the Republic of Moldova and reduce barriers between companies, institutions and markets. Through research, innovation and technology transfer we can build more efficient public services, more competitive companies and secure digital infrastructures. ICI Bucharest supports the development of joint projects and the exchange of expertise, so that technology becomes a real tool for economic integration and European rapprochement.” PEFA’s partner in the development of entrepreneurial dialogue in Chisinau, Carolina Bugaian, president of the Association of Women Entrepreneurs of Moldova – AFAM, spoke about the contribution of women to the development of the business environment: “The partnership between AFAM and PEFA offers women entrepreneurs from the Republic of Moldova and Romania access to a strong community, experience, contacts and new opportunities for collaboration. Women should not be seen only as beneficiaries of economic policies, but as leaders, investors and job creators. Through cooperation, mentoring and better access to finance, we can increase the number of women-led businesses and their contribution to the economy of the two states.” The second panel, dedicated to the development of bilateral relations between Romania and the Republic of Moldova, brought together leaders from the industrial and financial-banking sectors, representatives of the Romanian state institutions and partners from the Republic of Moldova. The discussions focused on investment opportunities, the identification of joint projects, the barriers faced by entrepreneurs and the development of mechanisms through which public institutions and the private sector can collaborate more efficiently. The participants discussed the need to continue the institutional and entrepreneurial dialogue and the importance of developing an active economic community, capable of transforming geographical proximity, historical ties and common values into economic and competitive advantages. By organizing the Romania-Republic of Moldova Economic Forum, PEFA reaffirms its commitment to facilitate cooperation between business communities, to support the internationalization of companies and to contribute to the development of an economic area increasingly connected to the European market and values. The Romania-Republic of Moldova Economic Forum benefited from the involvement of strategic, institutional partners and important companies from Romania and the Republic of Moldova, including: BCR, Garanti BBVA, maib, OTP Bank, Team Montage, Baumit, PPC, Austrotherm, Electrica, Moldcell, UP, Association for the Development of Domestic Entrepreneurship – ADAA, AES and DO Security. Institutional partners: Department for Sustainable Development, SME Romania and ICI Bucharest. Media partners: Antena 3 CNN, AGERPRES, Financial Intelligence, Club Economic, Economistul, CursDeGuvernare, Transilvania Business, Ziarul BURSA, I AM Sport, Știripesurse.ro, InvesTenergy, Profit.ro, News.ro, The Diplomat, EM360, Club Entrepreneur, Focus Energetic, Money.ro, Energy Industry Review, News One, V4Media and Iubim Brasovul Group. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Datacentres - UK UK government met 137 businesses over AI datacentres – but no environmental groups Investigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plans Aisha Down Global technology reporter Tue 27 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 03.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without any meetings with environmental groups, an investigation has found. The nonprofit organisation Spotlight on Corruption said a “considerable revolving door” shaped the government’s development of “AI growth zones”, a central plank of the former prime minister Keir Starmer’s AI and economic policy, with 38 ministers, senior civil servants and special advisers hired to positions in AI companies between July 2024 and September 2026. Meanwhile, even as top officials left government for jobs at OpenAI and Anthropic, government departments largely failed to engage meaningfully with stakeholders outside the technology industry. Kamila Kingstone, a campaign lead at the NGO, said: “The government totally failed at the most senior level to speak to environmental NGOs or community groups when developing its flagship policy on AI datacentres. This is despite the serious environmental implications of its plans.” Over 12 months, Spotlight on Corruption filed 40 freedom of information requests to 18 government agencies, seeking details of meetings and investment figures relating to the government’s policymaking on the growth zones, covering the period between July 2024 and June 2026. The investigation found that ministers, permanent secretaries and directors general involved in developing the policy met 137 businesses – some several times – to discuss Britain’s datacentre policy. By contrast, senior officials met only two community groups and no environmental organisations. View image in fullscreen Approval has been given for a £500m redevelopment of the Truman Brewery site in Brick Lane, east London, to include a datacentre. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Of the 38 senior officials who left government, nine were from the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, which has played a central role in shaping Britain’s AI strategy. These included a former minister for AI and intellectual property, a former AI adviser to the prime minister, a former director of AI opportunities, a deputy director of AI international policy and a head of AI engineering. AI growth zones were a groundbreaking policy under which the government promised to “ turbocharge the economy” and create jobs by building massive datacentres across five regions – in Starmer’s words, “mainlining AI into the veins” of the country. The policy aimed to pave the way for Britain to build big datacentres, some of them larger than any datacentre that has been built in the country so far. These developments, often partnered with US tech companies, would supposedly bring in thousands of jobs. Investigations by the Guardian have called the policy into question, suggesting that it rests on assumptions that do not hold up, financial figures that were not audited and exaggerated projections for job creation. In particular, the Guardian has shown there is little realism behind announced plans to power these developments, and claims that they will use purpose-built renewables. In fact, different government departments appear to diverge on how much electricity the UK’s datacentre plans will actually require – and what their environmental cost will therefore be. Meanwhile, there has been growing opposition to datacentres in Britain, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging from Auchtertool , a rural village north of Edinburgh, to Brick Lane in east London. View image in fullscreen Fourteen local campaigns rallied in September at Holyrood against datacentres planned in Scotland. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian Chi Onwurah, the MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the growing backlash – and the far larger opposition in the US – was a warning that the government needed to seek greater community input. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion “It is critically important that AI benefits communities and is also shaped by them,” she said. “I’ve been concerned about what we’ve seen in the US, where there’s a strong feeling that datacentres are being imposed without adequate consultation. We can see the backlash influencing the midterms. It’s really important that communities are involved in datacentres and AI growth zones and see the benefits.” Spotlight on Corruption’s investigation suggests that previous policy was largely shaped by conversations with business, and that the government “failed to take the environmental and social impacts [of datacentres] seriously”. While the government met a handful of civil society groups, these meetings were “held a few days before the launch of the policy, meaning they had no meaningful input”, according to the report. Finally, many further meetings between businesses and Starmer’s administration would not have been disclosed, said Spotlight on Corruption. This is largely because Starmer’s policy was led by a special adviser, Jade Leung, whose role was subject to far less stringent transparency requirements. Spotlight on Corruption also looked at how other countries – including Canada, Germany and Australia – developed policy. It found these countries consulted far more widely on introducing datacentres and had more stringent environmental criteria. It said the UK had “fallen behind equivalent jurisdictions” in developing an equitable strategy. A government spokesperson said: “We are clear that datacentres should create British jobs, strengthen supply chains and deliver benefits for the communities that host them, while prioritising clean power and using water responsibly – and meet with these companies to make sure that happens. We want to work closely with industry, local authorities, environmental groups and communities, and welcome opportunities to hear their views. “For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes. We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.” Explore more on these topics Datacentres - UK Planning policy AI (artificial intelligence) Computing Freedom of information news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Microsoft pulls out of AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concerns Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain Planning permission for new Scottish AI datacentres suspended for up to a year Labour rejects Zack Polanski’s call to ‘slam brakes’ on building AI datacentres Police Scotland warns ‘robust security’ needed to stop attacks on AI datacentres Datacentre projects face fees for grid access to ease connection queue, Ofgem says Scotland could freeze datacentre projects in challenge to UK’s AI strategy Datacentres using 6% of electricity supply in UK and US, research says Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland
